title: JPMorgan says Bitcoin could get more support than gold as ETF hedges unwind
body: JPMorgan says Bitcoin's hedging overhang could work in its favour against gold What happened JPMorgan analysts said in a note dated September 17 that Bitcoin could gain more support than gold if investors start unwinding the short positions and options currently used to hedge Bitcoin ETF holdings. The bank pointed to a gap in how the two ETF markets have recovered since inflows returned after the Federal Reserve's late-July meeting: gold ETFs have clawed back all of their earlier 2026 outflows, while Bitcoin ETFs have only recovered about half of theirs. The evidence behind the call is positioning data, not price action. Short interest in BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) remains close to its highest level this year, while short interest in the SPDR Gold Shares ETF (GLD) sits below its historical average. IBIT's put-to-call open interest ratio is also higher than GLD's, which JPMorgan reads as a sign that Bitcoin ETF investors are paying up for downside protection at a rate gold investors simply are not. Why it matters This is a mechanical argument about market positioning, not a fundamental case for Bitcoin over gold. JPMorgan's own framing is that Bitcoin still faces a more sceptical positioning backdrop than gold, likely due to more elevated hedging demand. The logic runs like this: a large pool of shorts and protective puts represents pressure that has to go somewhere.

title: Fed's unanimous hike stirs debate over how long high inflation persists
body: UBS's view that further hikes remain likely this year points to continued support for the US dollar and real yields, a combination that raises the opportunity cost of holding gold and could see some of August's ETF inflows unwind in the near term. Longer term, the bank argues gold's investment case remains intact, underpinned by rising global debt, an expected weaker dollar and the prospect of rate cuts next year. Other analysts framed the unanimous vote as evidence the Fed is taking a firmer stance against persistent inflation, much of it tied to elevated energy prices flowing from the conflict in the Middle East, with a further hike by year end widely seen as close to settled. Beyond that, views diverge sharply on how long above-target inflation could persist, with one long-term assessment suggesting price stability might not return for years given structural pressures from energy security, fiscal spending and the capital intensity of the AI investment cycle. -- The Fed hiked unanimously, but analysts can't agree on how long this inflation fight will last.

title: ICYMI: Trump tells Axios he's nearing a big decision on resuming Iran war
body: Trump's comments to Axios add a fresh layer of uncertainty to an oil market already struggling to price the war's trajectory, echoing JP Morgan's own admission this week that it has no clear baseline view for crude. A resumption of major US combat operations against Iran would raise the risk of further attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping, the scenario Saudi Arabia and Qatar are understood to have flagged when they helped persuade Trump to hold off in August. Conversely, any sign that Tuesday's meeting with Gulf leaders tilts toward renewed diplomacy could ease some of the risk premium currently built into oil prices, though traders are likely to treat that as a low probability outcome given Trump's repeated threats over recent months. With tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz still below pre-war levels despite the increased US naval presence, any escalation risk keeps a floor under prices even as the broader market leans on demand destruction rather than supply fears alone. --- Adam had the news on this earlier: Trump says he faces a "big decision" on whether to launch new attacks on Iran I'm doing a ICYMI here... UBS sees two more RBA hikes to 4.85% terminal rate after Bullock's comments
body: This second batch of Q&A comments (earlier) hardens the picture from Bullock's earlier testimony, with her saying inflation risks are skewed to the upside and that persistent inflationary shocks are hard to look through, language that leaves little room to read a pause into the September 28-29 meeting. Her comment that there is a general consensus the neutral rate has risen matters beyond this cycle, since a higher neutral rate implies the RBA's current policy setting is less restrictive than the headline cash rate alone suggests, supporting her earlier remark that the Board is thinking about whether policy is tight enough. Deputy Governor Hauser's line that the Board is totally committed to hitting the inflation target reinforces that message from a second voice. UBS's call for two more hikes to a 4.85% terminal rate is a meaningfully more hawkish path than the roughly 70 to 75% priced for a single September move, and if that view gains traction it points to further upside for the Australian dollar and short-end yields over the coming months. -- Bullock and Hauser are both talking like a hike is coming, and UBS thinks it won't be the last.

title: Bullock: RBA weighing whether policy is tight enough as oil pressures build
body: Bullock's Q&A comments read as a clear extension of her earlier committee testimony, where she said upside inflation risks flagged in August are now materialising, and they push the tone further toward a hike at the September 28-29 meeting. The explicit "higher for longer" framing on oil, paired with her comment that businesses are now more inclined to pass on cost increases, speaks directly to the pass-through risk the RBA has been watching closely, while her remark that the Board is thinking about whether policy is tight enough is about as direct a signal as a sitting Governor gives outside a post-meeting statement. Her characterisation of the housing price falls as not that significant removes a potential reason to hold off tightening further, since a softer housing market has previously been cited as a channel through which past hikes are working. Taken together, these comments support the roughly 70 to 75% probability already priced for a further 25 basis point increase, and arguably nudge it higher. --- Bullock is now openly asking whether RBA policy is tight enough, and that's about as clear a hike signal as it gets.

title: US sanctions Iranian crypto exchange BitBank over IRGC Hormuz bitcoin transfers
body: The designation adds a fresh layer of scrutiny to crypto's role in Iran sanctions evasion, a theme likely to keep pressure on exchanges and wallets with any exposure to Iranian-linked flows, even indirectly. It also touches the Hormuz corridor story directly, since the sanctioned Hormuz Safe Marine Services Authority is described as having used BitBank to process payments tied to its bitcoin-settled transit scheme for vessels crossing the strait, a scheme Iran had reportedly targeted for over $10 billion in revenue. For oil and shipping markets, the practical effect is incremental rather than immediate, since sanctions on a single exchange are unlikely to materially disrupt Iran's broader sanctions evasion infrastructure, but they add another data point to the pattern of US economic pressure running in parallel with the military standoff in the Gulf. Bitcoin's own price reaction has been muted, consistent with the market's now well established view that Iran-related designations move geopolitical risk premia more than crypto valuations. --- Washington has sanctioned an Iranian crypto exchange it says funnelled hundreds of millions in bitcoin to the IRGC.

title: Seven ways to value Bitcoin, from network adoption to stock-to-flow
body: Seven ways to value Bitcoin, according to Ned Davis Research Bitcoin has risen 26% over the past four months, and its climb last month came as senators debated the Clarity Act. Even after that legislation failed in the Senate, Bitcoin held onto most of those gains, according to Dow Jones Newswires (via MarketWatch). But the question of what Bitcoin is actually worth remains one of the more contested debates in markets, precisely because, unlike a stock or a bond, it has no cash flow, earnings, or balance sheet to anchor a valuation. Ned Davis Research's chief alternatives strategist, John Laforge, addressed that gap directly in a note published Wednesday, cited by Dow Jones Newswires, laying out seven distinct approaches to valuing the cryptocurrency, each suited to different circumstances and each with its own weaknesses. The firm's own longer-term view, separate from Laforge's methodology piece, sees Bitcoin reaching around $170,000 by 2030 and as high as $230,000 by 2035. Why it matters For readers newer to crypto, the value of walking through these methods is less about landing on a single "correct" price and more about understanding that different valuation lenses answer different questions, and mixing them up is a common source of confusion. A model built for the coming quarters is not designed to answer where Bitcoin sits in a five-year cycle, and a metric that reflects miner sentiment is not the same as one measuring investor demand.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.7065 – Reuters estimate
body: The fixing mechanism matters most right now because of what it has been signalling over recent weeks. The PBOC set its reference rate at the widest weak side deviation from market estimates in six months in late August, after the yuan touched a three and a half year high, a clear sign of discomfort with the pace of gains rather than the level itself. Traders should read this as the central bank applying the brakes rather than attempting to reverse the broader trend, since the yuan has still risen a meaningful amount against the dollar this year. The balancing act Beijing faces is straightforward: a stronger currency helps with capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness at a time when the domestic economy is showing renewed signs of softness. Watching the gap between the daily fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the more reliable ways to gauge PBOC intent in the days ahead.---The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and lately the message has been to slow down.Summary: The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, allowing the yuan to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the daily midpoint during onshore hours.

title: Bullock says upside inflation risks are materialising as Middle East bites
body: Bullock's acknowledgment that upside inflation risks flagged in August are now materialising, rather than merely a possibility, leans hawkish ahead of the Board's meeting in just over a week. Her explicit link between Middle East oil price gains and both direct and indirect inflation pass-through gives markets a clearer read on why a further hike remains live, even as she flagged that Australian growth is slowing. The Australian dollar could find some support from the hawkish tone, particularly the reference to other advanced-economy central banks also responding to the same global inflation shock, though the acknowledgment of softening housing and gradually easing labour market conditions tempers how far that repricing is likely to run. Overall, the testimony reads as consistent with, rather than a clear upgrade to, the roughly 70 to 75% probability already priced for a hike at the 28-29 September meeting. --- Background: Preview: RBA Gov. title: Yen Slips Ahead of BOJ Decision
body: The Japanese yen weakened beyond 156 per dollar on Friday, trading near a two-week low as investors awaited the latest Bank of Japan policy decision, with markets broadly anticipating an interest-rate hike. Market participants are also looking for guidance on the likelihood and pace of further tightening as policymakers confront rising inflation and wage growth, alongside pressure from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent for a more aggressive cycle of rate increases. In parallel, Japan's core inflation slowed to 1.7% in August from 1.8% in July, its first deceleration in four months. Still, expectations that price pressures could intensify in the coming months continue to underpin a hawkish outlook for the BOJ, with disruptions linked to the Middle East further heightening inflation risks. Earlier this month, the yen had risen to a seven-month high, driven by bets on more forceful BOJ tightening, recent joint intervention by Tokyo and Washington, and the prospect of increased capital repatriation by Japanese investors. title: Australian Dollar Attempts Rebound
body: The Australian dollar climbed above $0.71, rebounding from a recent four-week low as hawkish remarks from the Reserve Bank of Australia's governor strengthened expectations of further policy tightening. Governor Michele Bullock noted that upside inflation risks were starting to materialize and cautioned that rising costs could entrench inflation, citing the conflict in the Middle East, higher energy prices, and mounting domestic cost pressures. Before her testimony, swaps markets were pricing in at least two additional rate increases by the February meeting, with roughly an 87% probability that the first hike would occur on September 29. This represents a significant shift from early September, when traders anticipated just one more increase, likely by year-end. The Australian dollar also drew support from a weaker US dollar, declining US Treasury yields, and easing oil prices, while a rebound in global equity markets further bolstered the risk-sensitive currency. title: Japanese Shares Gain Ahead of BOJ Decision
body: The Nikkei 225 Index rose 0.9% to above 64,600 on Friday, advancing for a third consecutive session as investors positioned ahead of the Bank of Japan's latest policy decision, where a rate hike is widely anticipated. Markets are also seeking signals on the likelihood of additional tightening as policymakers confront persistent inflation and wage growth, alongside pressure from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Japan's annual inflation rate remained unchanged at 1.9% in August, while core inflation stayed below the BOJ's 2% target for the seventh straight month at 1.7%. Technology and AI-related shares led the market higher, mirroring overnight gains on Wall Street as worries about AI development safety risks receded. Standout performers included Kioxia (up 3.2%), SoftBank Group (4.1%), Advantest (4%), Lasertec (5.5%), and Ibiden Co (3.3%). The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: Gold Holds Gains on Lower Oil Prices
body: Gold hovered around $4,350 an ounce on Friday after gaining nearly 2% in the previous session, supported by a drop in oil prices that eased inflation concerns and helped drive bond yields lower. Crude declined for a third straight session as Saudi Arabia moved to restore flows through its East-West pipeline, while President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet with Gulf leaders next week. US Treasury yields also retreated from multi-year highs, with the 10-year yield slipping to around 4.93% after briefly topping 5% earlier in the week. At the same time, investors continued to evaluate the Federal Reserve's policy outlook following its first interest rate increase in three years. The US central bank indicated that further tightening may be required to contain inflationary pressures, and markets are now pricing in roughly a 53% chance of another move in October. title: Japan Food Prices Rise the Least in 25 Months
body: Japan's food prices rose 3.1% year-on-year in August 2026, easing from a 3.5% increase in July and marking the slowest pace of growth since July 2024. Price pressures softened across several categories, including fresh vegetables (5.5% vs 6.5% in July), fresh fruit (0.1% vs 2.4%), dairy products and eggs (1.3% vs 3.5%), cakes and candies (5.0% vs 6.1%), meats (3.3% vs 3.9%), alcoholic beverages (0.4% vs 0.6%), and prepared foods (3.3% vs 3.5%). Meanwhile, cereal prices declined for the fourth consecutive month (-3.4% vs -2.2%), and rice prices fell 15.7% year-on-year, extending their slide for a fourth month in a row and registering the steepest drop since April 2005. By contrast, price growth accelerated in several categories, including fish and seafood (9.9% vs 9.0%), oils, fats and seasonings (4.0% vs 3.4%), beverages (6.0% vs 5.5%), and meals eaten out (2.1% vs 1.7%). title: US Futures Steady After Upbeat Session
body: US stock index futures were little changed on Friday, pausing after a strong rally in the previous session driven by easing oil prices and lower bond yields, which buoyed risk appetite. On Thursday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 0.61%, the S&P 500 climbed 1.14%, and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.69%. Chipmakers led the move higher, extending a rebound after earlier concerns over AI safety had raised doubts about future AI-related capital expenditures. Standout gains came from Micron (up 5.5%), Nvidia (2.5%), Intel (7.7%), AMD (6.4%), and SanDisk (6.2%). Equities drew support from declining oil prices, which helped ease inflation concerns and fueled a broad-based rally in Treasuries. The yield on the US 10-year note retreated to around 4.93% after briefly moving above 5% earlier in the week. Sentiment on Wall Street was further lifted by relief that the Federal Reserve delivered a widely anticipated rate hike, even as policymakers signaled that additional tightening may be needed to bring inflation back under control. title: Japan Inflation Rate Stays at 7-Month High
body: Japan's annual inflation rate remained at 1.9% in August 2026, unchanged from July and still at its highest level since December 2025. Prices continued to rise across most categories, including food (3.1% vs 3.5% in July), transport (2.3% vs 2.6%), housing (1.0% vs 1.0%), household goods (4.9% vs 3.7%), clothing (1.5% vs 1.2%), healthcare (3.0% vs 2.1%), recreation (2.2% vs 1.9%), and miscellaneous items (0.7% vs 0.4%). Gasoline prices also accelerated (2.0% vs 1.8%), while electricity prices fell more sharply (-2.4% vs -0.1%), reflecting the impact of government energy subsidies. Education costs remained in deflation (-3.8% vs -3.8%). Core inflation, which excludes fresh food, eased slightly to 1.7% from 1.8% in July, staying below the Bank of Japan's 2% target for the seventh consecutive month. On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose 0.1%, a notable slowdown from the upwardly revised 0.5% increase recorded in July. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: Japan Core Inflation Eases, Below Forecasts
body: Japan's core consumer price index (CPI) — which excludes fresh food but includes energy — rose 1.7% year-on-year in August 2026, following a 1.8% increase in July. The pace of growth eased from July's six‑month high and came in slightly below market expectations of a 1.8% gain. Even so, core inflation remained under the Bank of Japan's 2% target for an eighth consecutive month, as government fuel subsidies continued to offset upward pressure from higher oil prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East. By contrast, the CPI measure that strips out both fresh food and fuel — a gauge the Bank of Japan regards as a better indicator of demand-driven inflation — climbed 1.9% year-on-year in August, matching the fastest increase in three months. At its July meeting, the Bank of Japan kept its benchmark interest rate at 1.0%, the highest level since September 1995. This followed a 25-basis-point hike in June, aimed at preventing rising oil prices from stoking broader inflationary pressures. On a year-over-year basis, the August reading reflects the same rate of price growth as in the prior month, underscoring a period of steady, moderate inflation. title: Japan's National Core CPI Eases to 1.7% in August, Slightly Below July Reading
body: Japan's National Core Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 1.7% year-over-year in August 2026, easing slightly from a 1.8% gain recorded in July 2026. The data, updated on 17 September 2026, indicate a modest slowdown in underlying inflation pressures. The National Core CPI measures price changes excluding volatile components and compares each month's level with the same month a year earlier. In this case, the August figure reflects how prices have changed versus August of the previous year, while the July reading was measured against July a year earlier. The marginal deceleration from 1.8% to 1.7% suggests that price growth remains relatively contained on an annual basis. Market participants and policymakers closely track core inflation for signals on the broader price trend, as it strips out short-term volatility. The latest figures imply that, at least for now, Japan's underlying inflation dynamics are stable, with no sharp acceleration in year-over-year price growth evident in the August data.
